title: One missed day
hookLine: missing a single day barely dented habit growth in that study
carry: after a missed day, return; don't restart

cards: A Tuesday goes sideways. The alarm doesn't go off, a kid wakes up sick, and the sit never happens. Wednesday morning, a small voice does the math: that's it, the chain is broken, might as well start over some other week.
That voice sounds a lot like discipline. Today asks whether it's telling the truth. Back on day one hundred fifty-five, this path gave a short answer.
The same study behind yesterday's curve gives the longer one: what does one missed day do to a habit that's still forming?

teach.h: DRAWING THE CURVE OF A HABIT.
teach.b: First, the study. Phillippa Lally and her colleagues asked volunteers to pick one new daily behavior, like drinking water with lunch or going for a run before dinner, and to report each day how automatic it felt.
Over the following weeks, the researchers drew the curve of each habit as it grew.

teach.h: ONE MISSED DAY BARELY DENTED IT.
teach.b: Second, the missed days. Not everyone showed up every day, so the researchers looked at what a gap did. Missing a single chance to do the behavior did not seriously set the habit back.
When people came back, the curve carried on climbing. That's today's word: the curve forgives. Third, the honest edge.
The study looked at single missed days. It doesn't promise that a month off costs nothing. One gap is a pothole; a long run of gaps is a different road.
So the finding isn't permission to stop. It's permission to start again tomorrow without starting from zero. Fourth, older voices saying something close.

Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor who kept a private notebook of reminders to himself, told himself not to be discouraged or disgusted when he fell short of his principles, but, when knocked back, to return to them again.
Jewish tradition has a word for coming back after straying: teshuvah, return. Different settings, the same small move. After a missed day, the useful question isn't how bad was that.
It's what is the smallest way back in.

how: People who use the habit research often treat a missed day as a pothole rather than a reset, and come back the next day with the same small practice instead of a bigger one to make up for it.

o: one missed day barely sets back a habit still forming
a habit is safe no matter how long you stop doing it
a missed day is fine as long as you do double the next

games.q: inside the curve forgives: tap the pairs.
p: drew the curve of new habits

s: miss one day and a new habit resets to zero
in Lally's study, a single missed chance didn't seriously set the habit back.
the study shows a long break costs nothing
it looked at single missed days; it doesn't promise a month off is free.
Marcus Aurelius told himself to return after falling short
his notebook urges him not to be discouraged, but to come back to his principles.

games.q: you planned a short sit every morning and missed yesterday. what does today's study point toward?
o: double today's sit to make up for it.
do today's sit as usual and keep going.
wait for a better week and start over.
games.why: one missed day barely dented the curve, and it kept climbing when people came back. the study says nothing about making up the day.

practice: During the sit the mind will wander, and each time is a missed moment, a tiny skipped day.

When you notice, skip the verdict, no sigh, no 'again?', and come back to the next breath, the way you'd step back onto a path after stepping aside to let someone pass. Count nothing; each return is the practice.

wordCard.voice: The curve forgives. One missed day barely dents a habit that's still forming; coming back matters more than the gap. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, from Jewish tradition: 'return,' the word for coming back after straying.

carryVoice: Your line: after a missed day, return; don't restart. A gap is a pothole, not the end of the road. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts & Wardle, "How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world"
